questions.title: Default Constructor Invocation
questions.question: Write a class with an explicit no-argument constructor that prints a notification message when an instance is created, and instantiate it from `main`[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: In Java, a constructor is a special block of code invoked when an object is instantiated using the `new` keyword[cite: 1, 24]. When a programmer explicitly defines a no-argument constructor, it overrides the compiler-provided default constructor[cite: 24]. At runtime, the JVM allocates memory for the new object on the heap, initializes all fields to their default zero-values, and calls the `<init>` method in bytecode[cite: 2, 6, 24]. The constructor body executes after the superclass constructor has finished[cite: 6]. This problem illustrates the exact execution lifecycle of instance creation and confirms how constructors serve as the entry point for custom initialization logic[cite: 24].
hints: Define a constructor with the exact same name as the class and no return type[cite: 24].
Place a `System.out.println` statement inside the constructor body[cite: 1, 24].
Instantiate the class inside `main` using the `new` operator: `new MyClass();`[cite: 1, 24].
questions.expectedOutput: Default constructor called

questions.title: Parameterized Field Initialization
questions.question: Write a `Person` class with a parameterized constructor that initializes `name` and `age` fields, and display their values using an instance method[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: Parameterized constructors allow objects to be initialized with specific states at the moment of creation, avoiding the need for multiple subsequent setter calls[cite: 23, 24]. The parameters passed to the constructor are received in local variable slots within the constructor's execution frame[cite: 6, 9, 24]. The constructor assigns these values directly to the object's instance fields on the heap[cite: 6, 24]. By binding data at instantiation time, classes can guarantee that required attributes are present before any instance methods are called, enforcing baseline object invariants from the very start[cite: 23, 24].
hints: Declare instance variables `private String name;` and `private int age;`[cite: 23].
Create a constructor `public Person(String name, int age)` that assigns values to the fields[cite: 23, 24].
Instantiate the object with arguments: `new Person("Akshat", 26);`[cite: 24].
questions.expectedOutput:
Name: Akshat
Age: 26

questions.title: Constructor Overloading Palette
questions.question: Overload constructors in a `Product` class by providing no-arg (default values), one-arg (name only), and two-arg (name and price) versions, and verify all three in `main`[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: Constructor overloading allows a single class to provide multiple ways to initialize an object, accommodating varying levels of initial information[cite: 24]. Like method overloading, constructors are overloaded by defining unique parameter lists—differing in parameter count, types, or order[cite: 9, 24]. During compilation, javac inspects the arguments provided at each `new` call site and resolves the matching constructor signature[cite: 9, 24]. This provides flexibility for callers, allowing default fallbacks when data is partially known while still supporting full initialization when complete data is available[cite: 24].
hints: Create a no-arg constructor that assigns default fallback values like `"Unknown"` and `0.0`[cite: 24].
Create a single-parameter constructor that sets the name while defaulting the price[cite: 24].
Create a two-parameter constructor that sets both name and price explicitly[cite: 24].

questions.title: Disambiguation with this Reference
questions.question: Write a class where constructor parameter names match instance field names exactly, and use the `this` reference keyword to resolve the shadowing collision[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: When a constructor or method parameter shares the exact identifier as an instance field, the parameter shadows the field within that lexical block[cite: 4, 6]. An unqualified assignment like `id = id;` simply assigns the parameter to itself, leaving the heap field uninitialized with its default value[cite: 2, 6, 24]. To resolve this shadowing collision, Java provides the `this` keyword, which represents a reference to the current object instance[cite: 4, 6]. Qualifying the target field as `this.id = id;` instructs the compiler to store the parameter value into the instance variable on the heap[cite: 4, 6].
hints: Declare instance variables such as `private int id;` and `private String title;`[cite: 4, 23].
Name constructor parameters identically: `public Item(int id, String title)`[cite: 24].
Assign using `this.id = id;` and `this.title = title;`[cite: 4, 23].
questions.expectedOutput: ID: 101, Title: Java Guide

questions.title: Collection Initialization in Constructor
questions.question: Write a `Team` class that initializes an internal `ArrayList` field inside its constructor and populates it with initial seed elements[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: Initializing collection fields inside a constructor ensures that an object is never in an invalid or half-initialized state with a `null` collection reference[cite: 2, 23, 24]. When the constructor runs, it allocates a new `ArrayList` on the heap and assigns its reference to the class's private field[cite: 2, 23, 24]. By instantiating collections in constructors, classes avoid `NullPointerException`s when methods attempt to add or iterate over elements later on[cite: 5, 7, 24]. This pattern guarantees that every new instance is immediately ready for operation with an allocated, usable collection[cite: 24].

In the constructor, instantiate the list: `this.members = new ArrayList<>();`[cite: 23, 24].

questions.title: This Constructor Chaining
questions.question: Chain constructors in a `Book` class using `this(...)` so that all secondary constructors delegate initialization to a primary master constructor[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: Constructor chaining within the same class using `this(...)` eliminates duplicated initialization code across constructor overloads[cite: 24]. When one constructor invokes `this(...)`, it delegates the initialization work to another constructor in the same class with a matching parameter signature[cite: 24]. Under Java Language Specification rules, `this(...)` must be the very first statement in the constructor body[cite: 24]. A common design pattern is to have simpler, secondary constructors provide default arguments and delegate to a single primary 'master' constructor, centralizing validation and field assignments in one place[cite: 24].

questions.title: Super Constructor Delegation
questions.question: Create a `Vehicle` base class with a parameterized constructor, and a `Car` subclass that calls `super(make, model)` to initialize inherited fields[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: In an inheritance hierarchy, a subclass constructor must invoke a constructor of its superclass before executing its own body[cite: 6, 24]. This ensures the inherited state is properly initialized[cite: 24]. If no explicit call to `super(...)` or `this(...)` is written, the compiler automatically inserts an implicit `super();` call to the no-arg superclass constructor[cite: 24]. However, when the base class defines only parameterized constructors, the subclass must explicitly call `super(arg1, arg2)` as its first statement[cite: 24]. This enforces bottom-up initialization order, guaranteeing that parent class fields are fully set up before the subclass runs[cite: 6, 24].

questions.title: Default Constructor Elimination
questions.question: Demonstrate that defining a parameterized constructor eliminates the compiler's default no-arg constructor, and fix the resulting subclass compilation issue by adding an explicit parent constructor[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: The Java compiler provides a synthetic, public no-argument default constructor only if a class defines no constructors at all[cite: 10, 24]. Once any constructor is explicitly declared (such as a parameterized constructor), the compiler ceases to generate the default constructor[cite: 24]. If a subclass then attempts to compile with an implicit `super();` call, compilation fails because the parent class no longer has a no-arg constructor[cite: 24]. To fix this, developers must either add an explicit no-arg constructor to the parent class or have the subclass explicitly call one of the parent's available parameterized constructors using `super(...)`[cite: 24].

questions.explanation: Constructors serve as the primary security checkpoint for object creation[cite: 24]. Relying on external code to validate parameters before instantiation is risky, as invalid data can produce corrupted objects[cite: 23, 24]. By adding validation guards directly inside the constructor body, invalid arguments are caught immediately[cite: 24]. If a precondition is violated (such as a negative age or a null name), the constructor throws an `IllegalArgumentException`[cite: 24]. This halts object creation before the reference is returned, ensuring that half-initialized or invalid instances never leak into the application[cite: 23, 24].

The no-arg constructor calls `this(1.0)`, which in turn calls the master constructor `this(1.0, 1.0)`[cite: 24]. Because `this(...)` must be the first statement in each constructor, execution transfers down the delegation chain to the master constructor first[cite: 24]. The master constructor's body runs to completion, after which control returns back up through each calling constructor in reverse order[cite: 6, 24]. When `new C()` is invoked, class $C$'s constructor is called first[cite: 6, 24]. Before executing any statements in its own body, $C$ invokes `super()`, calling class $B$'s constructor[cite: 6, 24]. Similarly, $B$ invokes `super()`, calling class $A$'s constructor[cite: 6, 24]. Class $A$ (extending `Object`) finishes first, followed by $B$, and finally $C$[cite: 6, 24]. questions.title: Copy Constructor with Deep Array Cloning
questions.question: Implement a copy constructor `Student(Student other)` that performs a deep copy of an internal mutable array field, ensuring the original and copy remain independent[cite: 5, 24].
questions.explanation: A copy constructor creates a new object using an existing instance of the same class as a template[cite: 24]. If the class contains mutable fields (like an array or a collection), performing a shallow copy (`this.scores = other.scores;`) simply copies the memory address, causing both objects to share the same underlying array[cite: 5, 23]. Mutating the array in the copy would then alter the original object's data as well[cite: 5, 23]. A proper copy constructor performs a deep copy by allocating a new array (`other.scores.clone()` or `Arrays.copyOf()`), ensuring the two instances are completely isolated in memory[cite: 5, 19, 24].

By making the constructor private and providing static factory methods with descriptive names (like `fromEpoch` and `fromIsoString`), the instantiation intent is clear[cite: 12, 24]. When a class defines multiple constructor overloads, each constructor must assign every final field[cite: 6, 24]. Having each overload initialize all fields independently can lead to code duplication and potential omissions[cite: 24]. Constructor chaining via `this(...)` solves this cleanly: secondary constructors delegate to a single primary constructor that performs all final field assignments in one place[cite: 24]. Writing an exception-safe constructor requires wrapping subsequent initialization steps in a `try-catch` block[cite: 24]. questions.title: Complete Instance Initialization Lifecycle Order

3. Before the master constructor's body executes, instance field initializers and instance initializer blocks run in their textual order of appearance[cite: 6].
4. The master constructor's body executes[cite: 24].

questions.title: Step Builder Pattern Constructor
questions.question: Implement a Step Builder pattern using chained interfaces and a private constructor to enforce mandatory field initialization at compile time in a strict step sequence[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: Standard builder patterns allow calling `.build()` at any point, which means missing mandatory fields can only be caught at runtime[cite: 24]. The Step Builder pattern solves this by using a series of nested interfaces that guide the caller through mandatory fields in a strict compile-time sequence[cite: 24]. Each step interface returns the next step's interface[cite: 24]. Only after all mandatory steps are completed does the builder expose the `.build()` method[cite: 24]. The underlying class uses a private constructor to ensure it can only be instantiated through this validated step sequence[cite: 10, 24].
hints: Define step interfaces: `interface NameStep { EmailStep name(String n); }` and `interface EmailStep { BuildStep email(String e); }`[cite: 24].
Have the internal builder class implement all step interfaces[cite: 24].
Make the main class constructor private so it can only be called by the builder's `build()` method[cite: 10, 24].
questions.expectedOutput: User: Akshat | Email: akshat@example.com

questions.title: Constructor Delegation Graph Cycle Resolution
questions.question: Demonstrate how circular constructor delegation (`this(...)` cycles) causes compilation errors, and implement a clean, acyclic delegation graph[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: Constructor delegation cycles occur when constructor $A$ calls `this(...)` to invoke constructor $B$, and constructor $B$ delegates back to $A$ (either directly or through an intermediate constructor)[cite: 24]. If allowed, this would cause an infinite loop during object construction that would overflow the stack[cite: 2, 6, 24]. The Java compiler detects circular constructor invocations and rejects them at compile time with a 'recursive constructor invocation' error[cite: 24]. To prevent this, constructor delegation graphs must form a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where all secondary constructors delegate toward a single master constructor[cite: 24].
hints: Note in comments that `A() { this(1); }` and `A(int x) { this(); }` triggers a compile error[cite: 24].
Design a clean DAG where each constructor overload delegates strictly toward the primary master constructor[cite: 24].
Ensure the master constructor does not call `this(...)`, terminating the delegation chain[cite: 24].
questions.expectedOutput: Config: localhost:8080 (SSL=false)

questions.title: Immutable Hierarchy with Complex Super Chaining
questions.question: Design an immutable subclass hierarchy where each layer contains `final` fields, defensive copies, and explicit `super(...)` constructor chaining[cite: 23, 24].
questions.explanation: Maintaining immutability across an inheritance hierarchy requires discipline at every level of the chain[cite: 5, 23]. Each class in the hierarchy must declare its fields as `private final`, validate preconditions, and make defensive copies of any mutable arguments passed to its constructor[cite: 5, 6, 23, 24]. When a subclass constructor is called, it must invoke `super(...)` to initialize the parent fields before initializing its own[cite: 6, 24]. By combining defensive copying with strict `super(...)` constructor chaining, the entire object hierarchy remains immutable once instantiated[cite: 23, 24].
hints: In `Asset`, declare `private final String id; private final Date acquired;`[cite: 5, 6, 23].
In `HardwareAsset extends Asset`, call `super(id, acquired);` using a defensively copied Date[cite: 5, 10, 24].
Return defensive copies from all getters across every level of the hierarchy[cite: 10, 23].
questions.expectedOutput: Asset ID: HW-101 | Serial: SN-99823

questions.title: Reflective Instantiation Safety Gate
questions.question: Write a singleton constructor that detects and blocks unauthorized reflective instantiation attempts using a static instantiation flag[cite: 10, 24].
questions.explanation: Standard singleton implementations can be compromised using Java Reflection[cite: 2, 10]. A client can access the private constructor via `Constructor.setAccessible(true)` and instantiate a second object, breaking the singleton guarantee[cite: 10, 24]. To defend against this, the private constructor can check a static instantiation flag[cite: 24]. The first instantiation—triggered during legitimate singleton initialization—sets the flag to `true`[cite: 24]. If reflective code attempts to call the constructor a second time, the constructor detects the active flag and throws an `IllegalStateException` or `SecurityException`[cite: 23, 24].
hints: Maintain a `private static boolean instanceCreated = false;` flag[cite: 24].
Inside the private constructor, check `if (instanceCreated) throw new IllegalStateException(...);`[cite: 23, 24].
Set `instanceCreated = true;` during the first valid instantiation[cite: 24].
questions.expectedOutput:
Standard singleton instance acquired: true
Security gate triggered: Reflective instantiation prohibited: singleton already exists
